title: “Health Is in the Air”: Visual and Olfactory Nudges and Food Choices at University Vending Machines
abstract: Background/Objectives: Ambient sensory cues can influence food choice, yet their role in everyday environments remains underexplored, with much of the existing evidence derived from laboratory studies. This is particularly relevant in university settings, where students often make rapid, convenience-driven choices that may be nudged toward healthier options by sensory cues (e.g., images or scents). Methods: A quasi-experimental field study was conducted across three consecutive one-week conditions: control, visual (a nature-themed poster), and olfactory (jasmine fragrance). Snacks were classified according to perceived healthiness ratings from a pre-study questionnaire. After predefined exclusions, purchases were analyzed using binary logistic regression, with condition as the main predictor and price and time of day examined as additional factors. Results: Among N = 1043 purchases, products classified as healthy were more frequent during the olfactory week than during the control and visual weeks. The visual condition did not differ significantly from control. Higher prices were associated with lower odds of purchasing a product classified as healthy, whereas time of day was not significantly associated with purchasing behavior. Conclusions: These findings provide field-based evidence suggesting that olfactory cues may be associated with a shift toward food choices perceived as healthier in vending-machine environments, pointing to their potential as a low-cost sensory nudging strategy while highlighting the need for confirmation through randomized or counterbalanced designs and replication across diverse real-world food-choice settings beyond university contexts.

claims.text: Products classified as healthy were purchased more frequently during the olfactory condition compared to the control condition.
Products classified as healthy were purchased more frequently during the olfactory condition compared to the visual condition.
Purchases of products classified as healthy during the visual condition did not differ significantly from the control condition.
Higher product prices were associated with lower odds of purchasing a product classified as healthy.
Time of day was not significantly associated with purchasing choices of healthy versus non-healthy products.

limitations.text: Much of existing evidence on sensory cues and food choice is derived from laboratory studies, leaving everyday settings underexplored.
The study relied on a quasi-experimental consecutive-week design rather than a randomized or counterbalanced design.
The intervention was conducted only within a university vending-machine environment, limiting generalizability across diverse real-world food-choice settings.

future_work.text: Confirming the sensory nudging findings using randomized or counterbalanced experimental designs.
Replicating sensory cue interventions across diverse real-world food-choice settings beyond university contexts.
